title: Heritage sites in Tamil Nadu: Chola temples, Mahabalipuram and Gingee
seo_title: Heritage Sites in Tamil Nadu: UNESCO Temples, Forts and More
meta_description: Heritage sites in Tamil Nadu: Mahabalipuram, the Great Living Chola Temples, Gingee Fort, the Nilgiri railway, Madurai, Keeladi and Adichanallur.
summary: Tamil Nadu shares in five UNESCO listings: the Group of Monuments at Mahabalipuram, the Great Living Chola Temples (Thanjavur, Gangaikonda Cholapuram, Darasuram), Gingee Fort within the Maratha Military Landscapes, the Nilgiri Mountain Railway and the natural Western Ghats. Add Madurai, Kanchipuram, Srirangam and Chidambaram, and the excavated sites of Keeladi, Adichanallur and Arikamedu.

sections.h2: Why Tamil Nadu is India's temple heartland
paras: Tamil Nadu has the longest unbroken temple tradition in India. Pallava kings at Kanchipuram and Mahabalipuram carved rock-cut shrines and built the first large structural temples in stone in the 7th and 8th centuries. The Cholas raised the great imperial temples of the 11th and 12th centuries, and later Pandya, Vijayanagara and Nayaka rulers expanded temple towns with vast gopurams, halls and tanks. Many of these temples remain in daily worship.

Behind the temples is a deep archaeological record: megalithic burials, Tamil-Brahmi inscriptions in rock shelters, Sangam-period towns and Roman-era trade at Arikamedu. Our guides to the [Chola dynasty](chola-dynasty.html) and [Indian temple architecture](indian-temple-architecture.html) give the background.

sections.h2: UNESCO World Heritage Sites in Tamil Nadu
paras: The Group of Monuments at Mahabalipuram (1984) includes the five rathas, the Arjuna's Penance relief, cave mandapas and the Shore Temple, mostly of the 7th and 8th centuries under the Pallavas. The Great Living Chola Temples were first listed in 1987 with the Brihadisvara temple at Thanjavur, built by Rajaraja I and completed about 1010, and extended in 2004 to include Gangaikonda Cholapuram and the Airavatesvara temple at Darasuram.

Gingee Fort in Viluppuram district is part of the Maratha Military Landscapes of India, inscribed in 2025, which covers twelve forts in Maharashtra and Tamil Nadu. The Nilgiri Mountain Railway joined the Mountain Railways of India listing in 2005, and parts of the Western Ghats in Tamil Nadu fall within that natural serial site of 2012. Our programme [Mamallapuram: rock-cut and structural temples](mamallapuram-rock-cut-and-structural-temples.html) is the best way to see the Pallava monuments with someone who can explain the sequence.

sections.h2: Ancient temples to see in Tamil Nadu
paras: Kanchipuram has the Kailasanatha temple, an early 8th century Pallava building, along with later Ekambareshvara and Varadaraja temples. Madurai's Meenakshi temple, mostly Nayaka in its present form, is a city within a city with towering gopurams. Srirangam's Ranganatha temple is enclosed by seven concentric walls, and Chidambaram's Nataraja temple is central to the history of Shaiva worship and dance. Rameswaram's corridors and Kumbakonam's many temples add more.

Before visiting, our lecture [Dravida temple architecture](dravida-temple-architecture.html) explains vimana, gopuram and mandapa so students can read what they see. The tour [South India temple architecture](south-india-temple-architecture.html) links the major sites into one itinerary.

sections.h2: Archaeological sites: Keeladi, Adichanallur and Arikamedu
paras: Keeladi in Sivaganga district, excavated by the ASI and then the Tamil Nadu State Department of Archaeology since 2015, has revealed brick structures, pottery inscribed with Tamil-Brahmi and evidence of an urban settlement of the early historic period. The dating of its earliest levels has been debated, and reports should be read with that in mind. A site museum at Keeladi displays the finds.

Adichanallur, near Tirunelveli, is a large urn-burial site of the Iron Age, first dug in the late 19th century and re-excavated recently. Arikamedu near Puducherry was a port with Roman and Mediterranean pottery from around the turn of the common era. Our lecture [Burials and bioarchaeology](burials-and-bioarchaeology.html) explains what urn burials can tell us.

Gingee's three hill citadels joined by walls show how successive powers, from Nayakas to Marathas, Mughals, French and British, used the same hills. Thirumalai Nayakkar Mahal in Madurai, Thanjavur's Maratha palace and Saraswathi Mahal library, Fort St George in Chennai and the Danish fort at Tharangambadi (Tranquebar) show later layers. Chettinad's mansions add a merchant community's architecture.

Our city guides cover walks in [Chennai](heritage-walk-in-chennai.html), [Madurai](heritage-walk-in-madurai.html), [Thanjavur](heritage-walk-in-thanjavur.html) and [Mahabalipuram](heritage-walk-in-mahabalipuram.html).

faq.q: How many UNESCO World Heritage Sites are in Tamil Nadu?
faq.a: Tamil Nadu shares in five listings: Mahabalipuram, the Great Living Chola Temples, the Maratha Military Landscapes of India (through Gingee Fort), the Mountain Railways of India (through the Nilgiri Mountain Railway) and the Western Ghats, a natural site. Only Mahabalipuram and the Chola temples lie wholly in the state.

faq.q: Which temples are in the Great Living Chola Temples listing?
faq.a: Three temples: the Brihadisvara temple at Thanjavur, the Brihadisvara temple at Gangaikonda Cholapuram and the Airavatesvara temple at Darasuram. They were built by Chola kings in the 11th and 12th centuries and are still in worship.

faq.q: What has been found at Keeladi?
faq.a: Excavations at Keeladi in Sivaganga district have found brick buildings, drains, wells, pottery with Tamil-Brahmi writing and objects pointing to an urban settlement of the early historic period. The dating of the earliest levels is debated, so read headline dates with care.

faq.q: Why is Gingee Fort a UNESCO site?
faq.a: Gingee is one of the twelve forts in the Maratha Military Landscapes of India, inscribed in 2025. It was held by the Marathas in the late 17th century, when Rajaram used it as a base, and shows how they adapted hill fortifications in the south.

faq.q: What are the oldest temples in Tamil Nadu?
faq.a: The rock-cut and structural temples of the Pallavas, from the 7th and 8th centuries, are the oldest surviving temples. Mahabalipuram's rathas and Shore Temple and the Kailasanatha temple at Kanchipuram are the best examples.

posts.hook: Thanjavur's great temple is over a thousand years old and still in worship.
posts.caption: Rajaraja I completed the Brihadisvara temple around 1010. Its walls carry long inscriptions listing gifts, staff and lands.

posts.hook: At Mahabalipuram, start with the rathas.
posts.caption: The five rathas are carved from rock as models of different temple types. Then walk to the Shore Temple to see the same ideas built in stone.
